en: Dhātukathā 2 Niddesa 2.4.
Exposition of the Fourth Method: The Comprehended and the Not Comprehended.
Those phenomena which are included by the truth of the origin,

and those phenomena which are included by the truth of the path— whether included by way of the aggregates, included by way of the bases, or included by way of the elements— and those phenomena which,
by means of those [former] phenomena, are included by way of the aggregates, included by way of the bases, [or included by way of the elements].
Those states included by way of inclusion under the element—by how many aggregates, by how many bases, and by how many elements are those states included?
Those states are included by one aggregate, by one base, and by one element.
As for those states [included] by the female faculty...
Those phenomena associated with the male faculty … those phenomena associated with the pleasure faculty … those phenomena associated with the pain faculty …
Those phenomena associated with the faculty of mental pleasure … those phenomena associated with the faculty of mental pain … those phenomena associated with the faculty of equanimity …
Those phenomena [associated] with the faculty of faith … those phenomena [associated] with the faculty of energy … those phenomena [associated] with the faculty of mindfulness …
The states [associated] with the faculty of concentration … the states [associated] with the faculty of wisdom … the states [associated] with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" …
Those phenomena associated with the faculty of final knowledge;
those phenomena associated with the faculty of one who has already known;
those phenomena associated with ignorance.
Those phenomena that [arise] with ignorance as condition through volitional formations;
those phenomena that [arise] with the six sense bases as condition through contact;
those phenomena that [arise] with feeling as condition through craving.
The phenomena that arise with craving as condition through clinging...
the phenomena that arise through kamma-existence...
the phenomena that arise through sorrow...
Those phenomena that arise through lamentation… those phenomena that arise through suffering… those phenomena that arise through mental distress…
Those phenomena through which one is overcome by distress...
those phenomena through which one is established in mindfulness...
those phenomena through which one is endowed with right exertion...
Those phenomena associated with the immeasurables … those phenomena associated with the five faculties … those phenomena associated with the five powers …
Those phenomena [associated] with the seven factors of enlightenment;
those phenomena [associated] with the noble eightfold path;
those phenomena [associated] with contact.
Those phenomena that [arise] through volition...
those phenomena that [arise] through resolve...
those phenomena that [arise] through attention...
Those phenomena [arising] from root-phenomena;
those phenomena [arising] from both root-phenomena and phenomena associated with roots;
those phenomena [arising] from both root-phenomena and phenomena associated with roots.
...from the taints ...
from the fetters ...
from the knots ...
...from the floods ...
from the yokes ...
from the hindrances ...
Those phenomena which, by way of misapprehensions … by way of clingings … by way of defiled phenomena … [are associated] with those phenomena …
Those phenomena which are included in the classification of aggregates by way of the defilements themselves and the phenomena associated with defilement;
those phenomena which are included in the classification of aggregates by way of the defilements themselves and the phenomena defiled by defilement;
and those phenomena which are included in the classification of aggregates by way of the defilements themselves and the phenomena associated with defilement.
Those phenomena that are included by way of the inclusion of bases (āyatana) and included by way of the inclusion of elements (dhātu)—
those phenomena which are included by those [same] phenomena through the inclusion of aggregates (khandha), the inclusion of bases, and the inclusion of elements—
by how many aggregates, by how many bases, and by how many elements are they included?
Those phenomena are comprised within one aggregate, one base, and one element.
There are two truths, fifteen faculties,
and eleven factors of dependent origination.
Furthermore, there are eleven above;
thus, the "Cluster" section here consists of thirty items.
This concludes the fourth exposition: the description of the term for what is included by way of inclusion.
